course.title: Music Appreciation: A History of Western Music
course.description: A guided tour of Western music from Gregorian chant to minimalism, built to teach you how to listen closely and describe what you hear. You will learn the elements of music, the major stylistic eras, and the composers who defined them. Structure and factual outline are adapted from the History of music article on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: The element of music concerned with the organization of sound in time is…
questions.explanation: Rhythm governs duration, beat, and meter -- how sound is placed in time. See 'The elements of music'.

questions.prompt: A melody is best described as…
options: the tone color of an instrument
a succession of single pitches heard as a line
questions.explanation: A melody is a horizontal sequence of pitches perceived as one coherent tune.

questions.prompt: Harmony refers to…
options: pitches sounding together, as in chords
the shape of the whole piece
questions.explanation: Harmony is the vertical dimension: notes stacked and sounded simultaneously.

questions.prompt: Timbre (tone color) is what lets you tell apart…
options: a loud note from a soft note
a fast passage from a slow one
a trumpet and a violin playing the same pitch
a major chord from a minor chord
questions.explanation: Timbre is the quality that distinguishes instruments even on an identical pitch and volume.

questions.prompt: Gregorian chant is generally…
questions.explanation: Chant is monophonic: one melody with no harmony or accompaniment. See 'The Medieval and Renaissance eras'.

questions.prompt: Which composer is most associated with the Baroque era?
questions.explanation: Bach (1685-1750) stands at the summit of Baroque style; the others belong to later eras.

questions.prompt: The four instrument families of a standard orchestra are strings, woodwinds, percussion, and…
questions.explanation: Brass completes the four families: strings, woodwinds, brass, and percussion.

questions.prompt: Dynamics in music means…
options: the changing degrees of loudness and softness
the key the piece is in
questions.explanation: Dynamics covers volume and its changes, from pianissimo (very soft) to fortissimo (very loud).

lessons.title: The elements of music
lessons.grammar_note: Keep the vertical and the horizontal straight: harmony is pitches stacked at one moment, melody is pitches laid out in a line over time.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name and recognize the building blocks every piece of music is made from -- rhythm, melody, harmony, timbre, texture, form, and dynamics -- and use the right word for each. Warm-up from the diagnostic: if a trumpet and a violin play exactly the same pitch at the same volume, which element still tells them apart? Hold that question; the answer is timbre, and by the end of this lesson you will be able to explain why. These seven terms are the vocabulary you will reach for in every later lesson, from medieval chant to minimalism, so it is worth getting them precise now rather than guessing later.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Rhythm is the placement of sound in time: the beat, the tempo (how fast), and the meter (how beats group, often in twos or threes). Melody is a succession of single pitches heard as one line -- the part you hum. Harmony is pitches sounding together, built into chords, supporting or coloring the melody. Timbre, or tone color, is what makes a flute sound like a flute and not a clarinet on the same note. Texture describes how many lines sound at once and how they relate: monophony is one line alone, homophony is a melody over chords, and polyphony is several independent lines woven together. Form is the large shape of a piece -- how sections repeat, contrast, and return. Dynamics is loudness and its change, from soft (piano) to loud (forte). Together these seven elements are the axes along which any performance can be described.

sections.heading: Key composers & works
sections.text: You can hear the elements isolated in famous pieces. For rhythm, the driving pulse of Ravel's Bolero rides one unchanging ostinato while the orchestration grows. For melody, the long singing line of the slow movement of Dvorak's New World Symphony is almost pure tune. For harmony, the rich chords of a Bach chorale show voices moving together. For timbre, Benjamin Britten's Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra parades each instrument's distinct color in turn. For texture, a round such as Frere Jacques turns one melody into interlocking polyphony. For dynamics, the sudden fortissimo chord in Haydn's Surprise Symphony is a famous jolt. These are not facts to memorize so much as reference points: when a term feels abstract, play the matching example and the definition becomes obvious to the ear.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which element changes when the same tune is played first on a piano and then on a saxophone? 2) A piece gradually gets louder across a whole minute. Which element is at work? 3) One singer performs a melody with no accompaniment: what texture is that? 4) Name the element that describes whether beats group in twos or threes. 5) A melody supported by block chords underneath is which texture? Answers: 1) Timbre -- the tone color changes while pitch and rhythm stay the same. 2) Dynamics (a crescendo). 3) Monophony. 4) Rhythm (specifically meter). 5) Homophony.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing melody and harmony. If you can hum it as a single line, it is melody; if several notes sound at once, that is harmony. Mistake: treating dynamics as tempo. Loud is not the same as fast -- a slow passage can be very loud, and a quick one can be whisper-soft. Mistake: calling any busy texture polyphony; true polyphony needs independent lines, not just a thick chord. Exit ticket: (a) What single element distinguishes two instruments playing the identical pitch at the identical volume? (b) Name the texture in which several independent melodic lines sound at the same time. Answers: timbre; polyphony.

lessons.title: How to listen actively, and the instruments of the orchestra
lessons.grammar_note: When you describe a piece, pin each observation to an element -- 'the strings enter softly' is timbre plus dynamics -- rather than reaching for vague praise like 'it sounds nice'.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Listen to a piece on purpose instead of letting it wash past, and describe what you hear using the four orchestral families and the seven elements. Warm-up: before reading on, picture a symphony orchestra on stage and try to name the four groups of instruments by where they usually sit. Active listening is a skill, not a talent -- it is built by asking the same handful of questions every time you press play: what is carrying the tune, what is supporting it, how is it changing, and what is the shape of the whole. By the end you will have a repeatable routine for describing any piece, which is exactly what the later history lessons will ask you to do.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A standard orchestra has four families. Strings (violin, viola, cello, double bass) usually sit at the front and carry much of the melody and warmth. Woodwinds (flute, oboe, clarinet, bassoon) add color and solo voices behind them. Brass (trumpet, French horn, trombone, tuba) bring power and weight. Percussion (timpani, snare, cymbals, and more) supply rhythm and punctuation. To listen actively, run a routine: first find the melody and ask who is playing it; second notice the accompaniment and the harmony under it; third track the dynamics and tempo as they change; fourth follow the form, listening for sections that repeat or return. Describing a piece well means naming these observations in plain terms: 'a soft clarinet melody over sustained strings, growing louder as the brass enter.' That sentence alone uses timbre, texture, and dynamics together.

sections.heading: Key composers & works
sections.text: Two works teach the orchestra by design. Benjamin Britten's Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra (1946) states a theme, then hands it to each family and instrument in turn, so you learn every timbre in a quarter hour. Sergei Prokofiev's Peter and the Wolf (1936) assigns each character a specific instrument -- the bird a flute, the duck an oboe, the cat a clarinet, the wolf the French horns -- so following the story trains your ear to recognize tone colors. For active-listening practice on a full form, the opening movement of Beethoven's Symphony No. 5 repeats a famous four-note motive so insistently that you can trace it returning through the whole movement. Use any of these as a first exercise: name the instrument, then the element, then the change.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) To which family does the cello belong? 2) To which family does the oboe belong? 3) In Peter and the Wolf, which instrument represents the bird? 4) Which family typically supplies the timpani and cymbals? 5) Turn this into element language: 'the trumpets blast out the tune very loudly.' Answers: 1) Strings. 2) Woodwinds. 3) The flute. 4) Percussion. 5) A brass melody (timbre) at a loud dynamic (fortissimo) -- naming timbre and dynamics.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling the piano a string or percussion instrument and arguing about it instead of just describing its role; in an orchestra it is usually treated as a color within the ensemble. Mistake: listening passively and then having nothing specific to say -- always run the routine and note at least one observation per element. Mistake: lumping the French horn with woodwinds because it looks mellow; it is brass. Exit ticket: (a) Name the four orchestral families. (b) What are the four questions of the active-listening routine? Answers: strings, woodwinds, brass, percussion; who has the melody, what supports it, how are dynamics and tempo changing, and what is the overall form.

lessons.title: The Medieval and Renaissance eras
lessons.grammar_note: Monophony means one line; polyphony means many independent lines. The Medieval-to-Renaissance story is largely the growth from the first to the second.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe how Western art music grew from a single sacred melodic line into rich multi-voice polyphony, and place Gregorian chant, early polyphony, and Palestrina on that timeline. Warm-up: recall from the diagnostic that Gregorian chant is a single unaccompanied melody -- what do you think had to be invented for several independent lines to sound together without clashing? The answer is a developing sense of counterpoint and consonance, and this lesson follows that invention across roughly a thousand years, from the chant of the early Church to the polished polyphony of the late sixteenth century.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Medieval music (roughly 500 to 1400) was dominated by the plainchant of the Christian Church, a monophonic, unaccompanied melody sung in Latin, traditionally linked by legend to Pope Gregory I and so called Gregorian chant. Over time musicians added a second line, then more, giving birth to polyphony -- the Notre Dame school in Paris (Leonin and Perotin) was an early center. The Renaissance (roughly 1400 to 1600) made polyphony flower: composers wove several equal voices together with growing control of smooth, consonant counterpoint, in sacred Mass settings and motets and in secular madrigals. Music printing, which spread after about 1500, helped these works travel. The era's ideal was a clear, balanced interweaving of lines in which the sacred text could still be understood -- a standard that the next generation held up as a model of pure vocal polyphony.

sections.heading: Key composers & works
sections.text: Gregorian chant itself is anonymous, a vast repertory gathered over centuries. In early polyphony, Perotin (active around 1200) at Notre Dame in Paris expanded two-voice writing to three and four voices. Guillaume de Machaut (around 1300 to 1377) was the leading composer of the late Medieval period. In the Renaissance, Josquin des Prez (around 1450 to 1521) was celebrated across Europe for expressive, balanced polyphony. The towering name for smooth sacred counterpoint is Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina (around 1525 to 1594), whose Pope Marcellus Mass became the textbook example of clear, singable polyphony in which every voice is independent yet the words remain audible. His style was later taught for generations as the model of strict counterpoint.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Is Gregorian chant monophonic or polyphonic? 2) Which city's cathedral school was an early center of polyphony around 1200? 3) Name the Renaissance composer most associated with smooth sacred counterpoint. 4) What is a Mass setting -- sacred or secular? 5) Roughly what centuries does the Renaissance cover? Answers: 1) Monophonic -- one unaccompanied line. 2) Paris (the Notre Dame school). 3) Palestrina. 4) Sacred, a setting of the Latin liturgy. 5) About 1400 to 1600.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming Gregorian chant has harmony; by definition it is a single line, which is exactly what makes added voices such a historic leap. Mistake: thinking Pope Gregory I composed the chant named for him; the attribution is traditional legend, not documented fact. Mistake: dating Palestrina to the Baroque; he is a late-Renaissance figure who died in 1594, before the Baroque began. Exit ticket: (a) What texture defines plainchant? (b) Whose Mass became the model of clear Renaissance polyphony? Answers: monophony; Palestrina (the Pope Marcellus Mass).

questions.prompt: Which word names the vertical dimension of music, where pitches sound together as chords?
questions.explanation: Harmony is pitches sounded simultaneously; melody is the horizontal line.

questions.prompt: The texture of several independent melodic lines sounding at once is called…
questions.explanation: Polyphony weaves independent lines together, the Renaissance ideal.

questions.prompt: To which instrument family does the French horn belong?
questions.explanation: Despite its mellow tone the French horn is a brass instrument.

questions.prompt: Gregorian chant is best described as…
questions.explanation: Chant is a single melodic line with no accompaniment.

questions.prompt: The Renaissance composer famous for clear, smooth sacred polyphony is…
questions.explanation: Palestrina's Pope Marcellus Mass is the classic model of Renaissance counterpoint.

questions.prompt: In the active-listening routine, after finding the melody your next question is…
questions.explanation: Step two is identifying the accompaniment and harmony under the tune.

lessons.title: The Baroque era
lessons.grammar_note: A fugue is a texture-and-form built on imitation: one subject, entering voice by voice. A concerto is a contrast of forces: soloist (or small group) against the full ensemble.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Recognize the Baroque style -- roughly 1600 to 1750 -- by its drive, ornament, and strong bass, and explain two of its signature forms, the fugue and the concerto. Warm-up: you met Bach as the Baroque's great name in the diagnostic; this lesson shows what he and his contemporaries actually built. If the Renaissance ideal was balanced vocal polyphony, the Baroque added a propulsive bass line and a taste for contrast and display. By the end you will be able to describe a fugue and a concerto in plain terms and name the era's three towering composers.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The Baroque era runs from about 1600 to Bach's death in 1750. Its music is built over a continuous bass line, the basso continuo, usually a keyboard plus a low instrument, which anchors the harmony. Baroque style loves energy, ornamentation, and dramatic contrast of loud and soft or solo and ensemble. Two forms matter most here. A fugue is a piece built by imitation: a short melody called the subject is stated by one voice, then answered by a second voice while the first continues, and so on, the voices overlapping in disciplined counterpoint. A concerto sets a soloist, or a small group, against the full ensemble, trading and combining material -- the version with a small solo group is the concerto grosso. Opera also took shape in this era, and the oratorio, a large sacred work for voices and orchestra, flourished.

sections.heading: Key composers & works
sections.text: Three names define the era. Johann Sebastian Bach (1685 to 1750) is its summit: the Brandenburg Concertos, the Mass in B minor, and The Well-Tempered Clavier, a collection pairing preludes and fugues in every key, are landmarks of contrapuntal mastery. George Frideric Handel (1685 to 1759), born the same year as Bach, worked in England and wrote the oratorio Messiah, whose Hallelujah chorus is among the most famous of all choral pieces. Antonio Vivaldi (1678 to 1741), an Italian priest and violinist, wrote hundreds of concertos; The Four Seasons is a set of four violin concertos, each depicting a season, an early and vivid example of music painting a scene. Together Bach, Handel, and Vivaldi show the era's range from intricate counterpoint to grand public drama.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is the short melody that launches a fugue called? 2) In a concerto, what two forces are set against each other? 3) Name the continuous bass-and-keyboard foundation typical of Baroque music. 4) Which Vivaldi work is a set of four violin concertos about the seasons? 5) Name Handel's most famous oratorio. Answers: 1) The subject. 2) A soloist (or small group) and the full ensemble. 3) The basso continuo. 4) The Four Seasons. 5) Messiah.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using 'fugue' for any busy contrapuntal passage; a fugue specifically builds by imitating a stated subject voice by voice. Mistake: thinking Bach and Handel never overlapped; they were born the same year, 1685, though their careers ran on different paths. Mistake: calling The Four Seasons a symphony; it is a set of concertos. Exit ticket: (a) What distinguishes a concerto's texture? (b) Who wrote The Well-Tempered Clavier? Answers: the contrast between a soloist (or small group) and the full ensemble; Johann Sebastian Bach.

lessons.title: The Classical era
lessons.grammar_note: 'Classical' has two meanings: loosely, all art music; strictly, the era of roughly 1750 to 1820. In this lesson it means the strict sense -- the age of Haydn, Mozart, and Beethoven.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the Classical style -- clarity, balance, and elegant phrasing, roughly 1750 to 1820 -- and explain its two central structures, sonata form and the symphony. Warm-up: the Baroque prized dense counterpoint and a driving bass; predict how a new generation might react against that. They turned toward clearer melodies with simple accompaniment and tidy, balanced phrases. By the end you will be able to outline sonata form in three parts and name the three giants of the era, including the figure who carried it across the threshold into Romanticism.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The Classical era, about 1750 to 1820, prized clarity, balance, and graceful melody over Baroque density. Textures became largely homophonic -- a clear tune over supporting chords -- in neat, symmetrical phrases. Its central design is sonata form, the standard plan for a movement: an exposition presents two contrasting themes in different keys, a development reworks and recombines that material through changing keys and tension, and a recapitulation brings the themes back, now reconciled in the home key. The symphony, a multi-movement work for orchestra (typically four movements), became the era's grandest form, with the first movement usually in sonata form. The string quartet -- two violins, viola, and cello -- became the prized medium of intimate conversation among equal voices. These structures gave composers a shared architecture that listeners could follow.

sections.heading: Key composers & works
sections.text: Joseph Haydn (1732 to 1809) wrote over a hundred symphonies and dozens of string quartets, earning the nicknames father of the symphony and father of the string quartet; his Surprise Symphony sets a famous sudden loud chord. Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (1756 to 1791) brought the style to effortless perfection across symphonies (No. 40 and the Jupiter), concertos, operas (The Marriage of Figaro, The Magic Flute), and chamber music. Ludwig van Beethoven (1770 to 1827) began firmly in the Classical style but expanded its forms with unprecedented power and length; his nine symphonies, especially the Fifth and the choral Ninth, stretch the era's architecture and open the door to the Romantic era that followed.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the three sections of sonata form in order. 2) How many movements does a typical Classical symphony have? 3) Which composer is nicknamed father of the symphony? 4) Name the four instruments of a string quartet. 5) Which composer bridges the Classical and Romantic eras? Answers: 1) Exposition, development, recapitulation. 2) Four. 3) Haydn. 4) Two violins, viola, and cello. 5) Beethoven.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using 'Classical music' loosely and then confusing the whole tradition with the specific 1750 to 1820 era; keep the two senses separate. Mistake: thinking the development section introduces brand-new tunes; it reworks the themes already heard in the exposition. Mistake: placing Beethoven entirely in the Romantic era; he began as a Classical composer and expanded the style from within. Exit ticket: (a) What happens in the recapitulation of a sonata-form movement? (b) Which three composers define the Classical era? Answers: the themes return, now in the home key; Haydn, Mozart, and Beethoven.

lessons.title: The Romantic era
lessons.grammar_note: Program music tells a story or paints a scene with instruments alone; absolute music is instrumental music that refers to nothing outside itself. The Romantics loved the first without abandoning the second.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the Romantic style -- emotional intensity, expanded forms, rich harmony, roughly 1800 to 1910 -- and explain program music and the art song. Warm-up: the Classical era valued balance and restraint; imagine loosening those bounds for the sake of personal feeling and storytelling, and you have the Romantic impulse. By the end you will be able to define program music, name the art-song tradition, and connect four major composers to their specialties, from the intimate piano miniature to the vast music drama of the opera house.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The Romantic era, roughly 1800 to 1910, put personal emotion, imagination, and the individual artist at the center. Harmonies grew richer and more chromatic, forms stretched longer, and orchestras grew larger. Composers wrote program music -- instrumental works that depict a story, scene, or idea, such as a symphony that narrates a drama or a tone poem that paints a landscape -- in contrast to absolute music, which has no stated subject. The art song, or lied in German, set poetry for solo voice and piano, treating the two as equal partners. The piano, now powerful and expressive, inspired a flood of character pieces and virtuoso display. Nationalism also stirred: composers drew on the folk songs and dances of their homelands. Opera expanded too, reaching its most ambitious form in the continuous, through-composed music drama.

sections.heading: Key composers & works
sections.text: Franz Schubert (1797 to 1828) was a master of the lied, writing hundreds of songs such as Erlkonig that fuse voice and piano into vivid storytelling. Frederic Chopin (1810 to 1849) devoted himself almost entirely to the piano, in nocturnes, etudes, and dances of great poetry and refinement. Richard Wagner (1813 to 1883) transformed opera into music drama, using the leitmotif -- a recurring musical idea tied to a character or theme -- across vast works such as the four-opera Ring cycle. Johannes Brahms (1833 to 1897) upheld Classical forms like the symphony while filling them with Romantic warmth and depth. Hector Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique is a celebrated example of program music, narrating an artist's obsessive dream across five movements.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is program music? 2) What is the German word for an art song for voice and piano? 3) Which composer is most associated with the solo piano miniature? 4) What is a leitmotif, and which composer is it tied to? 5) Which composer kept Classical forms alive within Romantic style? Answers: 1) Instrumental music that depicts a story, scene, or idea. 2) Lied. 3) Chopin. 4) A recurring theme tied to a character or idea, associated with Wagner. 5) Brahms.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming all Romantic music tells a story; much of it is absolute music with no program at all. Mistake: calling any recurring tune a leitmotif outside its dramatic context; the term describes themes bound to characters or ideas, most famously in Wagner. Mistake: treating Brahms as an anti-Romantic because he used Classical forms; he was a Romantic who worked within those forms. Exit ticket: (a) What is the difference between program music and absolute music? (b) Which composer built operas around leitmotifs? Answers: program music depicts a stated subject while absolute music does not; Wagner.

lessons.title: The twentieth century, modern music, and the roots of jazz and popular music
lessons.grammar_note: Tonality organizes music around a home key; atonality deliberately avoids any such center. Minimalism, by contrast, stays tonal but builds from steady repetition of small patterns.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe how twentieth-century composers broke from traditional tonality -- through dissonance, atonality, and later minimalism -- and trace the roots of jazz and popular music in the same era. Warm-up: every era so far reacted against the one before it; predict what composers around 1910 might do with the lush, chromatic harmony the Romantics handed them. Some pushed harmony until a home key dissolved entirely. By the end you will be able to place Stravinsky, Debussy, atonality, and minimalism, and explain where jazz came from.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Around 1900 the shared language of tonality began to fracture. Claude Debussy's impressionism used shimmering, unresolved harmonies and color for their own sake, loosening the pull of a home key. Igor Stravinsky's ballet The Rite of Spring (1913) unleashed pounding, irregular rhythms and harsh dissonance, famously causing an uproar at its premiere. Atonality went further, abandoning any tonal center; Arnold Schoenberg systematized it into twelve-tone technique, ordering all twelve pitches so none dominates. Later in the century minimalism reacted against that complexity, building hypnotic music from the gradual repetition and slow transformation of short patterns. Meanwhile a separate stream rose in the United States: jazz grew in the early 1900s from the blues and ragtime within African American communities, prizing improvisation, syncopation, and swing, and it became a foundation of modern popular music.

sections.heading: Key composers & works
sections.text: Claude Debussy (1862 to 1918) led musical impressionism with works like Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun. Igor Stravinsky (1882 to 1971) reshaped rhythm with The Rite of Spring. Arnold Schoenberg (1874 to 1951) developed atonality and the twelve-tone method. In minimalism, Steve Reich and Philip Glass built large works from repeating cells. On the popular side, ragtime pianist Scott Joplin (around 1868 to 1917) wrote the Maple Leaf Rag; the blues shaped countless later styles; and jazz founders such as Louis Armstrong (1901 to 1971) and Duke Ellington (1899 to 1974) carried improvisation and swing to the world. These streams -- experimental art music and vernacular jazz -- together define the sound of the modern century.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What does atonality deliberately avoid? 2) Which Stravinsky ballet caused a famous riot in 1913? 3) Name the method Schoenberg devised to organize atonal music. 4) From which two earlier styles did jazz chiefly grow? 5) Which composers are associated with minimalism? Answers: 1) A tonal center or home key. 2) The Rite of Spring. 3) Twelve-tone technique. 4) The blues and ragtime. 5) Steve Reich and Philip Glass.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating atonal and minimalist music as the same thing; atonality avoids a key center, while minimalism is usually tonal and repetitive. Mistake: calling all modern music dissonant; impressionism and minimalism can be gentle and consonant. Mistake: dating jazz to the mid-century; its roots in blues and ragtime reach back to the turn of the twentieth century. Exit ticket: (a) What is the core idea of minimalism? (b) Name the two styles that fed early jazz. Answers: building music from repeated, gradually changing short patterns; the blues and ragtime.

questions.prompt: A fugue is built by…
options: stacking block chords under a tune
stating a subject and imitating it voice by voice
repeating one short pattern for a long time
setting a soloist against the orchestra
questions.explanation: A fugue develops through imitation of its subject across entering voices.

questions.prompt: The three sections of sonata form, in order, are…
questions.explanation: Exposition presents the themes, development reworks them, recapitulation returns them in the home key.

questions.prompt: Program music is…
options: instrumental music that depicts a story or scene
music printed in a concert program
questions.explanation: Program music portrays a narrative, scene, or idea with instruments alone.

questions.prompt: Which composer is most associated with the leitmotif in opera?
questions.explanation: Wagner wove recurring leitmotifs through his music dramas such as the Ring cycle.

questions.prompt: Atonality is music that…
questions.explanation: Atonal music deliberately avoids a home key; Schoenberg systematized it as twelve-tone technique.

questions.prompt: Jazz grew chiefly out of which two earlier styles?
questions.explanation: Early jazz drew on the blues and ragtime in the early twentieth century.
